name: t-test
seoDesc: t-test: work out your result from the significance level α and the sample standard deviation s. A free statistics calculator with the formula, units and a…
summary:
Give the t-test calculator the significance level α and the sample standard deviation s and it returns the answer. It is built for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number.

Editing anything puts the results away until the next press of Calculate — change one value at a time and the updated answer tells you what that value was worth.

sections.title: How does the t-test calculator work?
sections.html:
The t-test calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (choose test type, the alternative hypothesis H₁ (Test setup) and the alternative hypothesis H₁ (Test setup)); then you type in the significance level α, the sample standard deviation s, the mean x̄₁ and the std. s₁.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the t-test calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

P-value=(t-score, degrees of freedom, (((choose test type < 2) ? ( alternative hypothesis H₁ ) : ( alternative hypothesis H₁ ))))
P-value=(t-score, degrees of freedom, alternative hypothesis H₁)
P-value=(t-score, (rounded down, ((size n₁ − 1) × (size n₂ − 1) × (size n₁ × std. s₂ + std. s₁ × size n₂ ^ 2) ÷ ((size n₁ ^ 2) × (std. s₂ ^ 2) × (size n₁ − 1) + (std. s₁ ^ 2) × (size n₂ ^ 2) × (size n₂ − 1)))), alternative hypothesis H₁)
Sample mean x̄=hypothesised mean μ₀ + sample standard deviation s × t-score ÷ the square root of (sample size n)
Mean x̄₂=mean x̄₁ − hypothesised mean difference Δ = μ₁ − μ₂ − t-score × (the square root of (-(-size n₁ × size n₂ × ((std. s₁ ^ 2) + (std. s₂ ^ 2)) + size n₁ × (-size n₁ × (std. s₁ ^ 2) + (std. s₁ ^ 2) + (std. s₂ ^ 2)) + size n₂ × ((std. s₁ ^ 2) − size n₂ × (std. s₂ ^ 2) + (std. s₂ ^ 2))) ÷ (size n₁ × size n₂ × (size n₁ + size n₂ − 2))))
Sample mean x̄=hypothesised mean difference Δ = μ₁ − μ₂ + sample standard deviation s × t-score ÷ the square root of (sample size n)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Choose test type set to one-sample, Alternative hypothesis H₁ set to μ ≠ μ₀, Approach set to p-value and Significance level α = 0.05. The calculator returns Sample mean x̄ = 41.6228 and Degrees of freedom = 9.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Sample mean x̄ = 41.6228 and Degrees of freedom = 9 should be roughly the size you expected from Choose test type set to one-sample and Alternative hypothesis H₁ set to μ ≠ μ₀.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The t-test calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the significance level α and the sample standard deviation s — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the t-test calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the significance level α and the sample standard deviation s, which is 19 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (6 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Sample mean x̄ = 41.6228. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the t-test calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
